metadata.note: Track ai-. REAL DATA: the six largest departments from Bickel, Hammel & O'Connell, Science 1975 (the table distributed as UCBAdmissions in R). All rates are DERIVED from the published counts in simpson_evidence.py, never transcribed as percentages. NO VERBATIM QUOTE from the paper appears on screen: the full text could not be retrieved to verify exact wording, so the authors' conclusion is paraphrased and attributed — see FACTCHECK. The reel is about the statistical mechanism and explicitly does NOT claim the data shows an absence of bias; B06 is built to say the opposite, that disaggregation relocates the question rather than closing it. The accompanying simulation establishes that a reversal requires a confounder; its numbers are deliberately NOT quoted on screen.

beats.narration_text: Privet. This is Jainil. In nineteen seventy-three, across Berkeley's six largest graduate departments, forty-four and a half percent of the men who applied were admitted — and thirty percent of the women. A clear gap. Then somebody looked department by department, and in four of those same six, women were admitted at a higher rate than men. Both of those are true at the same time. Today: how that happens, and what it actually means when it does.

send arms terracotta, running indicator spins

props.segment: Every Group Went The Other Way
props.command: Men were admitted more often overall, women more often in most departments. Which number is wrong?
output: They are answers to different questions.

beats.narration_text: Add the groups together and you can get the opposite. Not a rounding error and not a trick — a total and every single group inside it can point in different directions, and every one of those numbers is correct.

beats.narration_text: Here are the six largest departments. In A, women were admitted at eighty-two percent against men's sixty-two. In B, sixty-eight against sixty-three. D and F lean to women as well. Only C and E go the other way, and barely. Four of six. Then draw the line, and put the total underneath it: forty-four point five percent of men, thirty point four percent of women. Fourteen points, the other way.

show.event: legend sets: men in ink, women in terracotta
department rows land one at a time, each marking which side leads
four of six rows are marked WOMEN
the rule draws, separating the total from the rows
the total lands marked MEN — the opposite of the block above it

props.title: ADMITTED, BY DEPARTMENT · BERKELEY 1973
props.caption: Four of six departments favour women. The total favours men by 14 points.

beats.narration_text: The first thing that total hides is that these departments are nothing like each other. Department A admitted sixty-four percent of everyone who applied to it. Department F admitted six. That is not a difference of degree. Getting into F was ten times harder than getting into A.

show.event: title lands, axis sets
A's bar grows to 64.4 as it is named
B through E land in order, stepping down
F lands at 6.4 and takes the accent — a tenth of A
caption lands

props.title: ADMISSION RATE, EVERYONE WHO APPLIED
props.caption: Same university, same year. Ten times the difficulty from one end to the other.

beats.narration_text: And the two groups did not apply to the same places. The two easiest departments, A and B, took just over half of every application the men sent. Of the applications the women sent, those same two departments took seven percent. The women applied, overwhelmingly, to the departments that were turning nearly everybody down.

show.event: two cards land left to right
the men's card fills: 51% of applications to A and B
the women's card lands in terracotta: 7%
caption lands under both

props.title: WHERE THE APPLICATIONS WENT

cards.title: Women
lines: 72% applied to C, E or F.

props.caption: Nobody's admission rate changed. Only which queue they stood in.

beats.narration_text: So here is the test. Hold every department's decisions exactly as they actually were, and give the women the men's application pattern instead. Their admission rate goes from thirty point four percent to fifty-one point six. That is above the men's forty-four point five. A fourteen point deficit becomes a seven point surplus, and not one admissions decision changed.

show.event: title lands
the observed women's bar grows to 30.4
the men's bar grows to 44.5, visibly taller
the standardised bar grows past both to 51.6 and takes the accent
caption lands

props.title: SAME DECISIONS, DIFFERENT APPLICATION PATTERN
props.caption: Each department's own rates, reweighted to the men's application pattern.

beats.narration_text: Which is the part worth sitting with. The aggregate asked whether admissions committees were biased, and the departments answered no. But that does not close the question — it moves it. The authors of the original study said as much themselves: what then needs explaining is why the women were applying to the most crowded and least funded departments in the first place. The reversal did not dissolve the problem. It relocated it, upstream, somewhere the total could never have shown you.

show.event: the first stage card springs up: the aggregate's question
arrow draws, the department answer lands
arrow draws, the third stage lands and fills terracotta
the terracotta note under it: the aggregate cannot see this

props.title: WHAT THE SPLIT ACTUALLY SETTLED
props.caption: Disaggregating moved the question upstream. It did not answer it.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. Take a metric your team reports as one number, split it by the biggest segment you have, and ask whether any segment moves the opposite way to the total — and what would have to be true for that to happen. Run it on a number you actually report to somebody. If the segments disagree with the headline, you do not have one result that needs explaining. You have two questions, and only one of them is about the thing you were measuring.
